claims.text: In single-phase refractory BCC high-entropy alloys, edge dislocations provide the dominant contribution to hardness and strength.
Edge-dislocation dominance governs the unusual retention of strength at intermediate high temperatures.
Between approximately 673 K and 1073 K, thermal activation promotes super-jogging on edge dislocations.
Super-jogs impede edge-dislocation motion and counteract ordinary thermal softening.
NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is an appropriate example of a single-phase refractory BCC HEA for the proposed test.
Temperature-dependent tensile or nanoindentation testing coupled with TEM or neutron diffraction can measure mechanical response and dislocation evolution over the proposed temperature range.
A refractory BCC HEA has exhibited an approximately temperature-independent strength interval between 673 K and 1073 K.
Edge dislocations can be prevalent and dominant relative to screw dislocations in a BCC high-entropy alloy.
The proportion of edge dislocations increases as temperature rises.
At lower temperatures, dislocation motion in refractory BCC HEAs is restricted by local energy barriers.

In multi-principal-element BCC alloys, both edge and screw dislocations can move by nanoscale segment detrapping from local energy barriers rather than solely by the conventional screw-dislocation kink-pair mechanism.
Super-jog formation preserves yield strength and therefore hardness, producing an intermediate-temperature plateau.
The tested HEA will show a pronounced yield-strength and hardness plateau between approximately 673 K and 1073 K.
In situ characterization will show an increasing fraction of edge dislocations over the plateau interval.
In situ characterization will reveal thermal super-jogging events correlated with the strength plateau.
BCC systems controlled by traditional screw-dislocation mechanisms should soften continuously as temperature increases.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase, compositionally complex refractory BCC HEAs.
The mechanism may not govern multiphase alloys in which interphase-boundary strengthening or precipitation hardening dominates.
Local chemistry and processing-induced microstructural differences may alter the transition temperature and the relative contributions of edge and screw dislocations.
Absence of the 673–1073 K mechanical plateau, or failure to observe increased edge-dislocation fraction and super-jog occurrence in that interval, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
